claims.claim: Usain Bolt was born on 21 August 1986 (body, FAQ, person.json birthDate)
claims.note: Both sources give 21 August 1986.

claims.claim: Born in Sherwood Content, Trelawny parish, Jamaica; FAQ calls it a village in the north of Jamaica
claims.note: Olympics.com says Sherwood Content, Jamaica. Britannica places it in Trelawny parish and calls it a town. 'Village' and 'nord' are loose, since Trelawny is in the north-west, but acceptable.

claims.claim: Nationality: Jamaica (person.json)
claims.note: Olympics.com lists Jamaica.

claims.claim: In August 2009 in Berlin Bolt ran 9.58 in the 100 m and 19.19 in the 200 m
claims.note: WA confirms 9.58 at the Berlin World Championships. Yahoo confirms 19.19 on 20 August 2009 in Berlin.

claims.claim: Four days between the two records; 100 m on 16 August, 200 m final on 20 August
claims.note: Yahoo says 20 August and 'four days earlier'. WA implies 16 August.

claims.claim: At the Tokyo 2025 Worlds both marks still stood
claims.note: The WA record watch lists 9.58 and 19.19 (Bolt, 2009) as the world records.

claims.claim: In 2002, aged 15, he won the 200 m at the World Junior Championships
claims.note: Britannica says he was 15 and won 200 m gold. Olympics.com says 'by the age of 16, in 2002', so the sources differ. The article picks 15 without noting this. 15 is consistent with his 21 August birthday and a July 2002 meet.

claims.claim: His first 100 m world record dates from May 2008
claims.note: Britannica: 9.72 in New York about four weeks after 3 May 2008. Olympics.com wrongly says 2007; the article correctly follows Britannica.

claims.claim: In Beijing he lowered the 100 m record to 9.69
claims.note: WA calls 9.69 the Beijing record set exactly one year before 16 August 2009.

claims.claim: He won the Beijing 200 m a few days later in 19.30, a world record; the Jamaican relay, with Bolt, also won gold with a world record
claims.note: Britannica gives world records of 9.69, 19.30 and 37.10 in Beijing.

claims.claim: In January 2017 the IOC disqualified the team: Nesta Carter's sample from those Games contained methylhexanamine, a banned stimulant
claims.note: ITV (opened via search result because the direct fetch hit the tool limit): the IOC announced on 25 Jan 2017 that Carter tested positive for methylhexaneamine and Jamaica was disqualified. The 'sample taken during those Games' detail is implied by the retest.

claims.claim: The official record shows eight Olympic titles, not nine (body, summary, FAQ)
claims.note: Olympics.com shows 8G. ITV says he had 'nine Olympic golds' before the stripping.

claims.claim: Tyson Gay was second in 9.71, a US record
claims.note: WA: Gay 9.71, a national record.

claims.claim: In the 200 m final he won by 0.62 s; the board first showed 19.20 before being corrected
claims.note: Yahoo: 0.62 s margin, initial time 19.20 revised to 19.19. It does not say 'tableau d'affichage', a minor embellishment.

claims.claim: He took 0.11 s off his own 100 m record in Berlin
claims.note: WA confirms 0.11 s off 9.69.

claims.claim: He won the 100 m and 200 m again at London 2012 and Rio 2016; first to win the Olympic 100 m at three consecutive Games
claims.note: Britannica and Olympics.com confirm both.

claims.claim: Summary: he retired after the 2017 Worlds; eight Olympic golds over three Games
claims.note: Britannica and Olympics.com confirm both.

claims.claim: Present-tense 'still holds' claims replaced by: World Athletics still listed both as world records in its record preview for Tokyo 2025
claims.note: Dated to the source; no present-tense claim remains in summary, opening or closing line.

claims.claim: January 2017: the IOC disqualified Jamaica's 2008 relay team; Nesta Carter's sample tested positive for methylhexaneamine; Bolt had to relinquish his medal
claims.note: ITV page opened in this re-check (25 Jan 2017): IOC, Carter, methylhexaneamine, 'has had to relinquish his medal'.

claims.claim: 12 August 2017, anchor leg of the 4x100 final, hamstring injury, fell; Britain won gold; retired with 14 World Championship medals
claims.note: Al Jazeera page opened: 12 Aug, anchor leg, hamstring, forward roll, Britain 37.47, '14 world career medals'.

claims.claim: Daegu 2011: false-start disqualification under the IAAF's immediate-disqualification rule; Blake won in 9.92
claims.note: Al Jazeera 2011 opened: immediate disqualification rule, Blake 9.92. 'Newly introduced/shortly before' timing removed.

claims.claim: Berlin 200 m on 20 August 2009 in 19.19 by 0.62; time first recorded as 19.20 then revised
claims.note: Yahoo opened: 20 Aug, 19.19, 0.62 margin, initial 19.20 revised. 'Scoreboard' wording removed.

claims.claim: Cricket coach encouraged him to take athletics seriously
claims.note: Olympics.com opened: 'his cricket coach encouraged him to take up athletics seriously'.

claims.claim: Added: Kingston 2002, youngest male world junior champion in any event; Athens 2004 hamstring, out in 200 m heats; Olympic 100 m record in London; Rio first to win both individual sprints at three straight Olympics; 1.96 m and the tall-sprinter belief
claims.note: Britannica opened in this re-check; all stated there.

claims.claim: Quote: 'I stopped worrying about the start. The end is what's important'
claims.note: Olympics.com opened: quote verbatim (translated in non-English versions, marked as such).

claims.claim: 'Two fastest sprint times in history' / 'same stadium' / 'north of Jamaica' wording removed
claims.note: Now 'two world records in the same city, four days apart', which WA and Yahoo support.

valueNote: Clear timeline from Trelawny to London 2017, explains the eight-not-nine Olympic golds with the IOC ruling, the Daegu false start and the 19.20/19.19 correction, with dated record status.
summary: Re-check after fixes. 7 flagged claim(s) from the previous review were corrected or removed: Every flagged claim was fixed or removed and the sources the previous check could not open (ITV, Al Jazeera 2011/2017, Yahoo, Star Tribune, Olympics.com, Britannica) were opened in this re-check; the page was expanded with Britannica and Olympics.com facts.
